content: Reliable phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) methods are available for rifampicin (RIF), isoniazid (INH), fluoroquinolones (FQs), bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), linezolid (LZD), amikacin (AMK), and delamanid (DLM). Testing algorithms that utilize culture and phenotypic DST are outlined in the relevant World Health Organization (WHO) policy framework and technical manual. Member states must ensure the capacity for DST for drugs used in treatment, provided reliable testing methods are available. Phenotypic DST methods are not reliable for ethambutol (EMB), ethionamide/prothionamide, cycloserine/terizidone, or imipenem-cilastatin/meropenem. Therefore, results from these tests should not be used for clinical decision-making. If resistance is suspected during treatment and DST is unavailable, the strains should be referred to a WHO supranational reference laboratory (SRL) for further testing. Material transfer agreements and import/export permits may be required. Currently, phenotypic DST for BDQ and LZD is limited in many settings, and resistance levels are likely low. BDQ is a core drug for drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) treatment and is included in the revised definition of extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB). If resistance is suspected during treatment and DST is unavailable, strains should be referred to an SRL for further testing. Treatment initiation should not be delayed while awaiting DST results. Patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) should be promptly started on an appropriate treatment regimen according to national guidelines. WHO recommends a shorter, all-oral BDQ-containing treatment regimen lasting 9–12 months. If molecular and phenotypic testing are performed in the same laboratory, one specimen may suffice. If testing is conducted in two laboratories, two specimens should be collected, and molecular and phenotypic testing should be performed in parallel. Sputum specimens or isolates should be transported to the appropriate testing laboratory if necessary. Low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) or second-line line-probe assays (SL-LPAs) should be used to detect mutations associated with FQ resistance. If these tests detect mutations linked to FQ resistance, MDR/RR-TB patients should be placed on an individualized longer regimen designed using the WHO priority grouping of medicines. The Xpert MTB-XDR test provides results for INH, ethionamide, and AMK and can inform individualized regimen selection. If low-complexity automated NAAT or SL-LPA results are negative for FQ resistance mutations, patients should continue on the all-oral BDQ-containing shorter MDR-TB regimen while awaiting phenotypic DST results. In settings with high underlying prevalence of FQ resistance or for patients at high risk of resistance, a specimen should be referred for culture and phenotypic DST for FQs. Phenotypic DST should include testing for resistance to the FQs used in the country and moxifloxacin at the clinical breakpoint to inform individualized drug selection. Regimens should be modified as necessary based on phenotypic DST results. Culture and phenotypic DST should be performed for each drug included in the treatment regimen for which accurate and reproducible methods exist. Reliable phenotypic DST methods are available for BDQ, FQs, CFZ, pyrazinamide (PZA), and INH when performed in a quality-assured laboratory. A WHO-approved molecular test for PZA resistance detection is available but is currently limited to use on culture isolates. If the isolate is susceptible to all drugs, the patient should continue on the preferred MDR-TB regimen. If resistance is detected to any drug, the patient should be placed on an individualized longer MDR-TB regimen designed using the WHO priority grouping of medicines. As phenotypic DST results are slow, patient response should be reassessed when these results become available. Monthly monitoring is essential, and patients should be closely followed up. WHO recommends that all patients treated with an MDR-TB regimen be monitored for treatment response using sputum culture and sputum-smear microscopy. Sputum culture should ideally be repeated at monthly intervals. Although the risk of treatment failure increases with each additional month without bacteriological conversion, no discrete cut-off point has been defined as a reliable marker of a failing regimen. The choice of cut-off point will depend on the clinician’s desire to minimize the risk of failure and limit the risk of prolonging a failing regimen. For patients with isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible tuberculosis (Hr-TB), rapid detection and placement on effective treatment regimens are critical to prevent the spread of Hr-TB and the acquisition of resistance to additional drugs such as RIF. The recommended Hr-TB treatment regimen includes RIF, EMB, PZA, and levofloxacin (LFX) for six months. Molecular DST for FQs should be performed for each patient with Hr-TB. The low-complexity automated NAAT can simultaneously detect INH and FQ resistance. PZA resistance detection should also be performed where available and quality-assured. Patients with FQ-resistant Hr-TB may be treated with a six-month regimen of (H)REZ or an individualized Hr-TB regimen. Detection of FQ resistance, along with PZA resistance, is important for patients with Hr-TB to ensure effective treatment and prevent amplification of resistance to RIF or FQs. Phenotypic DST for PZA is desirable if a quality-assured reliable DST for PZA has been established in the country. When resistance to PZA is confirmed, appropriate treatment regimens may need to be designed individually, especially if resistance to both FQ and PZA is detected.
